newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE papers critical of Ekeus tour, U.S. policy.
newsitem.headline: UAE papers critical of Ekeus tour, U.S. policy.

text.p: United Arab Emirates newspapers on Tuesday lashed out against U.S. policy on Iraq and accused the U.N. official in charge of eliminating Iraq's mass destruction weapons of serving "masters" in Washington.
The official, Rolf Ekeus, is touring Gulf Arab states in what diplomats said is an effort to drum up financial support for his commission, set up after the 1991 Gulf War.

"(Ekeus's) fame is widespread on an international level for his role in the continued siege on Iraq, and on an Arab level... for implementing U.S. policy on Iraq and not U.N. resolutions," Al-Khaleej daily said in a front-page editorial.
The Arabic-language paper said Ekeus's tour only served to weaken all Arab states.
"He wants us to implement the policies of his masters, to be partners in...the further weakening of Iraq when it has become clear that Iraq's weakness is weakness to all Arabs," it added.
Al-Bayan daily voiced similar sentiments in its front-page editorial, and accused the United States of killing thousands of children by supporting an embargo on Iraq.

"The United States knows well that a siege on Iraq does not weaken the Iraqi government, but it definitely kills thousands of Iraqi children," it said. "The United States...seeks to partition the Arab world by partitioning Iraq," it added.
The English-language Khaleej Times said the United Nations was a "hostage" to U.S. President Bill Clinton's domestic political concerns.

The local media comments, which analysts said reflected the official position, came only two days after UAE Foreign Minister Rashid Abdullah al-Nuaimi said that Iraq's military weakness had created a military and strategic imbalance in the Gulf region.
In Kuwait, the first stage of his trip, Ekeus said his commission needed $30 million in 1997 and if it was closed, there would no longer be any control over Iraq's military programme.
Ekeus went on a similar Gulf Arab tour before a Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) summit last year to ask for $90 million for three years to finance his commission.
The request drew fierce criticism from GCC member Qatar, which blasted the U.N. for treating the oil-rich Gulf states like bankrollers for its global operations.
